---
title: "Individualized"
author: "DK"

categories: [understanding]
---

Modern life depends on categorization.

We label, sort, and organize the world around us—not merely for convenience, but as a foundational tool for science, research, and progress.

Yet when we apply this same practice to human beings, the logic begins to break down.

To reduce a person to a label does not yield understanding; it imposes human-created boundaries, stripping away the uniqueness that defines that person and prematurely limiting their potential.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Professor H likes to quote Ecclesiastes:[^1]

[^1]: Ecclesiates 1:9

> "There is nothing new under the sun."

Labeling and sorting to organize society has been in practice for as long as humans have gathered, often with chilling results.[^2]

[^2]: Sima, Q. (1993). Records of the Grand Historian: Han dynasty (B. Watson, Trans.). Columbia University Press

In the final years of the Qin dynasty, the powerful court official Zhao Gao (赵高) wanted to test the extent of his control over the emperor and the court. He brought a deer before the Second Emperor, Qin Er Shi (秦二世), and deliberately presented it as a horse.

When the emperor laughed at the assertion, Zhao Gao turned to the court officials and demanded they confirm his identification.

Some stayed silent, while others—seeking favor—agreed that it was indeed a horse.

Those who dared to insist it was a deer were later executed.

The goal was not accurate classification; it was using a forced label as a tool of total submission.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This struggle over identity and control reaches back even further.

The Bible records that there was a war in Heaven (Revelation 12:7–9), with modern revelation clarifying that the conflict was fought over the agency of humankind—the fundamental right to choose good or evil.

The methods across the centuries may have evolved, but the ultimate objective remains unchanged: using labels and classifications not to understand people, but to sort, constrain, and control them.

The danger lies in evaluating people through aggregate measures—broad buckets, social classifications, and summary statistics.

Clayton Christensen observed in *How Will You Measure Your Life?*, relying on aggregate data may help us manage complex systems, but it fails when assessing the worth of a human being.

Real understanding does not happen on a balance sheet or through a demographic tag; it occurs at the level of the individual.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Our mothers knew it, and our fathers supported it: each child born into this world brings a unique heritage and a singular gift.

It is not for society to simplify a child's existence by assigning labels and classifications, no matter how noble its intent.

Rather, it is the primary role of the family—with society in a supporting role—to see that the child is brought up in the fear of the Lord, so that they may understand their own purpose.

In doing so, we will look past the convenience of labels and restore what forced classification seeks to erase: human dignity, individual agency, and the infinite capacity of a single life.
